subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the order and degree of the differential equation [d²y/dx² + (dy/dx)³]^(6/5) = 6y.

insider_note: Order and degree are read only after the equation is free of fractional and negative powers of any derivative — the very first move is always to clear those, as this equation's own 6/5 power shows.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Remove the fractional power
steps.margin_note: One mark. Raise both sides to the power 5/6 to clear the fractional exponent outside the bracket.
steps.memory_tip: A bracket raised to power p/q clears by raising both sides to the reciprocal power q/p.
lines: Raising both sides to the power 5/6:
steps.why: Raising both sides to the reciprocal power 5/6 clears the fractional exponent outside the bracket, leaving an equation written as a polynomial in the derivatives, which is what the order and degree are read from.
common_mistakes: Trying to read the order and degree directly from the fractional-power form without clearing it first.
Raising both sides to the power 6/5 instead of its reciprocal 5/6.

steps.label: State the order and degree
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Degree is read from the exponent of the HIGHEST order derivative only, never from a lower-order term.
steps.memory_tip: Degree only ever looks at the highest-order derivative's own exponent — every other term in the equation is irrelevant to it.
lines: The highest order derivative present is d²y/dx²,
The exponent of d²y/dx² in the cleared
steps.why: Order counts the highest derivative appearing in the equation, and degree is the power of that highest derivative once the equation is a polynomial in all the derivatives — here d²y/dx² appears to the first power alone.
common_mistakes: Confusing the outer exponent 6/5 in the original equation with the degree, instead of clearing it first.
Reading the degree from the (dy/dx)³ term instead of from the highest-order derivative d²y/dx².
